key_findings.claim: Electron Inversion Layer at Buried Interface (Polarization-Type)
key_findings.detail:
Under 800 V/50°C in anoxic conditions, a polarization-type failure occurs:

- Na⁺ accumulates at the glass/FTO interface (front of device), not penetrating deeply into the perovskite bulk (blocked by the built-in field of the p-i-n structure)
- The positive charge at the front interface **attracts electrons** at the buried perovskite/HTL interface (electrostatic coupling through the thin perovskite layer)
- An **electron inversion layer** forms at the buried interface, disrupting hole transport to the HTL
- Interface recombination increases, reducing photocurrent collection

Evidence from Kelvin Probe Force Microscopy (KPFM) and conductive AFM (C-AFM):
- Work function decreases at the buried interface (indicating electron accumulation)
- Local conductivity increases at grain boundaries
- Young's modulus increases by 5–10 GPa at grain boundaries (Na⁺-induced hydrogen bonding)
- [[papers/Wiley-45-301-2-s2.0-105008480848-2025-J-Failure Analysis of Polarization-Type Potential-Induced Degradation of Perovskite Solar Cells.pdf#page=4|Li et al. (2025), p.4]]

At higher voltage (1000 V) and/or elevated humidity, Na⁺ penetrates deeply into the perovskite layer:

- Na⁺ forms NaI and NaIBr compounds at grain boundaries and interfaces throughout the perovskite layer
- These create conducting inhomogeneities (shunt paths) across the cell
- Large dark regions (20–80% of cell area) visible in EL imaging, indicating extensive shunting
- Complete failure (Voc → 0) in 7/8 cells after 1000 h at 1000 V negative bias
- [[papers/Wiley-190-1756-2-s2.0-85121464246-2022-J-Are Perovskite Solar Cell Potential-Induced Degradation Proof?.pdf#page=3|Brecl et al. (2022), p.3]]

Simultaneously with Na⁺ ingress from the front, Ag⁺ ions from the rear silver electrode migrate into the perovskite:

- Ag⁺ forms AgI bonds — **more stable** than NaI (harder to reverse)
- Ag⁺ diffuses into the perovskite/ETL interface region
- Creates stable recombination centers at the rear junction
- [[papers/Wiley-141-1314-2-s2.0-85153703868-2023-J-Study of Potential-Induced Degradation in Glass-Encapsulated Perovskite Solar Cells under Different .pdf#page=5|Nakka et al. (2023), p.5]]

key_findings.claim: Halide Segregation Under Elevated Stress (60°C, 60% RH)
key_findings.detail:
Under elevated temperature and humidity, additional bulk degradation occurs:

- **PbI₂ formation** detected by XRD — a well-known perovskite decomposition product
- PbI₂ nucleates at grain boundaries and interfaces, blocking charge transport
- PL emission red-shifts by **22 nm** (vs. 8 nm at room conditions), indicating iodine-rich phase separation
- PL intensity quenches by **> 62.5%** (indicating dense nonradiative recombination centers)
- [[papers/Wiley-141-1314-2-s2.0-85153703868-2023-J-Study of Potential-Induced Degradation in Glass-Encapsulated Perovskite Solar Cells under Different .pdf#page=4|Nakka et al. (2023), p.4]]

Under 800 V/50°C:

- **Stage 1 (0–20 h):** Diode-like J-V preserved; primarily Jsc and FF losses (charge transport disruption at buried interface); PCE drops to 68.56% of initial
- **Stage 2 (20–100 h):** J-V curves become nearly linear (severe shunting-like behavior); FF collapses to 33% of pristine; PCE drops to 20.91% of initial; Voc remains relatively stable throughout both stages

- [[papers/Wiley-45-301-2-s2.0-105008480848-2025-J-Failure Analysis of Polarization-Type Potential-Induced Degradation of Perovskite Solar Cells.pdf#page=5|Li et al. (2025), p.5]]

- **Polarization-type (PID-p):** Partial recovery to 62.97% of original PCE after 47 days of dark storage
- **Shunting-type (PID-s):** Recoverable via positive voltage application (Na⁺ driven back to glass) if damage is not too severe
- **Elevated stress (ESC):** Very poor recovery (~10% efficiency retained) because PbI₂ formation is largely irreversible; only ~10% of degradation recovers vs. 58% at room conditions
- [[papers/Wiley-141-1314-2-s2.0-85153703868-2023-J-Study of Potential-Induced Degradation in Glass-Encapsulated Perovskite Solar Cells under Different .pdf#page=6|Nakka et al. (2023), p.6]]
